v: Don’t enter expecting a detailed ‘Human Computer’ origin story. As a portrait of a genius struggling with ordinary family relationships, though, it becomes a real treat — powered by effortless Vidya Balan and terrific Sanya Malhotra.
e: Shakuntala Devi is less interested in explaining how its subject became a mathematical phenomenon than in exploring what happened when an extraordinary personality collided with the expectations of parents, husband and daughter. That choice may disappoint viewers seeking a conventional biopic, but Vidya Balan and Sanya Malhotra make the personal story strongly engaging.
body:
If you are watching Shakuntala Devi expecting a detailed account of the hard work, challenges and effort that turned her into the Human Computer, you may be disappointed.

This is not really that kind of biopic.

Instead, the film is much more interested in the ups and downs of a genius trying to live among ordinary relationships — with her parents, husband and daughter.

And if you approach it from that angle, you are in for a treat.

The director makes that intention clear almost from the first scene itself.

What stayed with me most is the way the film explores a strange contradiction around highly successful people.

Millions of outsiders may admire and celebrate them, yet the people closest to them can experience an entirely different version of the same personality.

That aspect reminded me a little of the emotional conflict in My Father Gandhi.

Vidya Balan absolutely nails the role, as expected.

She moves effortlessly through Shakuntala Devi’s confidence, flamboyance, vulnerability, stubbornness and emotional contradictions.

Sanya Malhotra supports her with a terrific performance and gives the mother-daughter conflict the emotional weight it needs.

Amit Sadh and Jisshu Sengupta have comparatively limited space, but both make their presence felt.

And while plenty of noise is often made about who represents female-centric Hindi cinema, Vidya Balan has quietly been doing that work for years without needing to announce it every time 🙏

So, as a conventional mathematical-genius biopic, Shakuntala Devi may leave some questions unanswered.

As a film about the complicated personal life behind that genius, it worked very well for me.

v: Patience compulsory 😄 The Lucknowi slang and sloooow narration may test you, but survive that hurdle and Amitabh vs Ayushmann turns a landlord-tenant squabble into a deliciously desi Tom-and-Jerry ride.
e: Gulabo Sitabo asks the viewer to adjust to its deliberate pace and strongly local Lucknowi flavour before its pleasures begin to reveal themselves. Once that rhythm clicks, Amitabh Bachchan and Ayushmann Khurrana become two wonderfully petty pillars holding up a sharp landlord-versus-tenant comedy.
body:
You need patience — and a little passion — to enjoy Gulabo Sitabo.

The first hurdle is the strongly Lucknowi dialect.

For a large section of the audience, it may take some time to tune into the language and understand every exchange naturally.

The second hurdle is the sloooow narration 😄

The film is in absolutely no hurry, and that pace can seriously test your patience in the opening stretch.

But if you cross those two barriers, the reward is an excellent little ride powered by Amitabh Bachchan and Ayushmann Khurrana.

Story-wise, it is essentially landlord versus tenant — almost a desi Tom and Jerry setup, only with property, greed and wonderfully petty human behaviour replacing the cartoon traps.

The film also lands a few genuinely good roasts along the way.

On screen, Mirza and Baankey keep trying to outsmart and overshadow one another.

In reality, Amitabh and Ayushmann are doing the exact opposite: they support the story like two major pillars and make the constant bickering enjoyable.

Performances of this level are almost a cakewalk for both of them.

And I do not think I had ever seen Amitabh Bachchan in such a deliciously kameena avatar before 😛

Gulabo Sitabo will definitely not work for everyone.

But if you can surrender to its language, rhythm and deliberately small-scale conflict, there is a lot to enjoy in this strange little battle over an old haveli.

v: A beautifully simple salute to the faces we all recognise but rarely remember by name. No melodrama, no commercial decoration — just Sanjay Mishra carrying a painfully real story to a wonderfully written climax. MUST WATCH.
e: Kaamyaab turns the invisible life of Hindi cinema’s character actors into a warm, bittersweet and remarkably restrained film. Sanjay Mishra carries the entire journey with ease, while Hardik Mehta resists melodrama and lets the final irony — that even the finest sidekick remains overshadowed by the hero — land naturally.
body:
If you are open to a non-commercial film with a simple storyline and excellent performances, Kaamyaab is a MUST WATCH.

In roughly an hour and a half, the movie gives us a glimpse into the lives of the countless character actors and sidekicks who have appeared in hundreds of Hindi films without ever becoming household names.

We know their faces.

We have seen them as smugglers, policemen, doctors, villains, henchmen and fathers.

Yet many of us would struggle to name them.

There is something both funny and sad about the fact that the age of social media can suddenly make these forgotten performers recognisable again because one expression or scene becomes a meme.

Kaamyaab understands that strange afterlife beautifully.

Sanjay Mishra is terrific and carries the entire film on his shoulders.

The role fits his ability to make an ordinary man’s smallest disappointment feel completely real.

What I appreciated just as much is that director Hardik Mehta never tries to force melodrama into the story.

The world remains grounded and believable throughout.

Even the climax is written with wonderful restraint.

The final idea is both simple and painful: no matter how well a side actor performs, and no matter how much the audience enjoys him, the spotlight will almost always move back towards the HERO.

That is what makes Kaamyaab more than merely a film-industry story.

It is a heartfelt salute to generations of performers who helped make our movies memorable while remaining almost invisible themselves 🙏

v: A very familiar family-love-story template with one important difference: the couple happens to be two men. It sits awkwardly between message movie and full comedy, but the cast makes the subject feel refreshingly normal and easy to watch.
e: Shubh Mangal Zyada Saavdhan deliberately treats its same-sex romance like the most ordinary Bollywood family conflict possible. That simplicity is both its strength and limitation: the film never becomes a hard-hitting message drama or an all-out comedy, but Ayushmann, Jitendra and the ensemble make a still-taboo subject accessible without melodrama.
body:
MAN!!! Is there any genre Ayushmann Khurrana cannot do with ease?

Story-wise, Shubh Mangal Zyada Saavdhan is actually a very familiar Bollywood love story.

Two people fall in love.

The family does not approve.

In the second half, one partner enters the other partner’s family world and tries to win everybody over.

Eventually we move towards the classic “Jaa Simran jaa… jee le apni zindagi” territory 😄

The major difference, of course, is that the lead pair are two men.

Writer-director Hitesh Kewalya makes an interesting choice with that subject.

He does not turn homosexuality into a heavy melodramatic issue packed with giant message dialogues.

But he also does not make the movie an out-and-out family comedy in the way something like Dream Girl was.

As a result, the film lands somewhere in between.

It is neither a powerful message-oriented drama nor a complete laugh riot.

That middle ground limits the impact a little for me.

At the same time, the approach has one major advantage: the relationship itself begins to feel wonderfully normal.

All the actors are very good, and the characterisations help make a subject that was still treated as taboo by many viewers feel simple and watchable even for a mainstream family audience.

That normalisation may actually be more useful than repeatedly announcing the film’s social importance.

So do not enter expecting too much from the plot or comedy and you are likely to enjoy it.

And for those of us who have spent years thumping our chests about Ayushmann’s script choices… yes, he gives us one more film to brag about 😄
